passages.t: Justice at the palace, and the king who will not return
passages.happening:
God sends Jeremiah down to the palace to speak to the king on David's throne, his officials and his people (verses 1 and 2). ‘Administer justice and righteousness. Rescue the victim of robbery from the hand of his oppressor’ (verse 3). They must not wrong the foreigner, the fatherless or the widow, or shed innocent blood (verse 3). If they do this, kings will keep riding through these gates (verse 4). If not, God swears by himself that the palace will become rubble (verse 5).

The palace is like Gilead and the summit of Lebanon to God, but he will make it a desert (verse 6). Destroyers will cut down its finest cedars (verse 7). The nations will ask why God did this to the great city, and they will be told: because they forsook the covenant and served other gods (verses 8 and 9).

‘Do not weep for the dead king; do not mourn his loss. Weep bitterly for the one who is exiled, for he will never return to see his native land’ (verse 10). That is Shallum son of Josiah, who has gone and will die where he was taken (verses 11 and 12).
passages.hearers:
Cedar from Lebanon was the prestige building material of the ancient world. Solomon's palace hall was even called the House of the Forest of Lebanon. That is why God speaks of the palace as Lebanon and Gilead, the land's great forests.

The dead king of verse 10 is Josiah, killed in 609 BC at Megiddo when he confronted Pharaoh Necho II. His son Shallum, better known by his throne name Jehoahaz, reigned three months before Necho deposed him and took him to Egypt, where he died. The people should not weep for the good king who died, but for the son who would never come home.

The chapter goes through Josiah's successors one by one. Each is measured by the same standard: justice for the robbed, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow.
passages.later: Kings tells the end of Shallum, or Jehoahaz: ‘Neco took Jehoahaz and carried him off to Egypt, where he died’ (2 Kings 23:34). Micah sums up the same demand: ‘to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God’ (Micah 6:8).
passages.asks: The king's palace would stand or fall on whether he did justice. Ask what in your life stands or falls on how you treat the weak. And ask what it means to weep for the exile rather than only for the dead.

passages.t: Woe to the king who builds with unpaid labor
passages.happening:
‘Woe to him who builds his palace by unrighteousness, and his upper rooms without justice, who makes his countrymen serve without pay, and fails to pay their wages’ (verse 13). He says he will build a great palace with spacious rooms, cut windows in it, panel it with cedar and paint it red (verse 14).

‘Does it make you a king to excel in cedar? Did not your father have food and drink? He administered justice and righteousness, and so it went well with him’ (verse 15). ‘He took up the cause of the poor and needy, and so it went well with him. Is this not what it means to know Me?’ (verse 16), says the LORD. But this king's eyes and heart are set on dishonest gain, innocent blood, extortion and oppression (verse 17).

So concerning Jehoiakim son of Josiah: no one will lament him with the mourners' cries (verse 18). ‘He will be buried like a donkey, dragged away and thrown outside the gates of Jerusalem’ (verse 19).

Jerusalem is told to go up to Lebanon and Bashan and cry out, for her allies are crushed (verse 20). God warned her when she was secure, and she would not listen (verse 21). Her shepherds will be driven off, and she will groan like a woman in labor (verses 22 and 23).
passages.hearers:
Jehoiakim was set on the throne by Pharaoh Necho in 609 BC and reigned until 598 BC. Judah was paying heavy tribute to Egypt, and yet the king built himself a grand new palace with forced, unpaid labor. Red paint, vermilion, was a luxury.

Verse 16 is one of the great sentences in the prophets. Josiah ate and drank like any king, but he took up the cause of the poor, and that, God says, is what it means to know him. Knowing God is not only a feeling or a belief. It is justice done for the needy.

Proper burial with lament was a basic honor. The mourners' cries for a king were traditional. Jehoiakim would have none, and be thrown out like a dead animal.
passages.later: The law said, ‘You must not withhold until morning the wages due a hired hand’ (Leviticus 19:13). James warns the rich, ‘the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you’ (James 5:4).
passages.asks: God says that taking up the cause of the poor is what it means to know him. Ask whether your knowledge of God can be seen in how you treat the poor. And ask whether anyone has worked for you and not been paid what they were owed.

passages.t: Coniah, the signet ring pulled off
passages.happening:
God swears that even if Coniah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were a signet ring on his right hand, he would pull him off (verse 24). He will hand him to Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans (verse 25) and hurl him and his mother into another land, where both will die (verse 26). They will never return to the land they long for (verse 27).

‘Is this man Coniah a despised and shattered pot, a jar that no one wants?’ (verse 28). ‘O land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD’ (verse 29).

God says to record this man as childless, a man who will not prosper in his lifetime, ‘None of his descendants will prosper to sit on the throne of David or to rule again in Judah’ (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Coniah is Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah. He became king at eighteen, reigned three months, and surrendered Jerusalem to Nebuchadnezzar in 597 BC. He and his mother were taken to Babylon.

A signet ring bore its owner's seal and was pressed into clay or wax to sign documents. It was the most personal and precious ring a king had. God says that even if Coniah were that close, he would pull him off.

Record him as childless does not mean he had no children. Chronicles lists his sons. It means that none of them would reign. The line of kings would be broken.
passages.later: After the exile God reverses the picture for Coniah's grandson: ‘I will make you like My signet ring’ (Haggai 2:23). Matthew's genealogy of Jesus runs through him: ‘Jeconiah was the father of Shealtiel’ (Matthew 1:12).
passages.hard:
If no descendant of Coniah would sit on David's throne, how can Jesus, whose genealogy in Matthew runs through him, be the son of David who reigns?

Readers have noticed this since early times, and several answers are offered. One notes that Matthew traces Jesus' legal descent through Joseph, who was not his biological father, while Luke's genealogy (Luke 3:23-38) runs through Nathan, another son of David, bypassing Coniah; many hold that Luke gives Mary's line or Joseph's natural line, though that too is debated. A second points to verse 30 itself: the sentence is on his lifetime and his immediate descendants, and none of Coniah's sons or grandsons, Zerubbabel included, ever reigned as king. A third notes that the curse seems softened after the exile, when God calls Coniah's grandson Zerubbabel his signet ring (Haggai 2:23), reversing verse 24, and that Jesus reigns not from an earthly throne in Jerusalem but as the risen king.

These answers can be held together, and all agree that the promise to David was kept by God's act rather than by the merit of David's sons.
passages.asks: Coniah was pulled off like a ring, and later his grandson was called God's signet ring. Ask what it means that God's judgment on one generation was not his last word on the family. And ask how you hear the cry, land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD.
